title: Spaghetti alla Carbonara
short_description: Roman pasta bound with egg yolk and pecorino — never cream.
full_description: The whole dish turns on one trick: the pan comes off the heat before the yolks go in, so they thicken into a glossy sauce instead of scrambling. Starchy pasta water does the rest of the work, loosening the eggs and emulsifying the rendered pork fat into something that clings to every strand. Four ingredients, no cream, and about fifteen minutes.

steps.text: Bring a large pan of well-salted water to the boil and drop in the spaghetti.
While it cooks, dice the bacon and render it slowly in a dry frying pan until the fat runs and the edges crisp.
Beat the egg yolks with the grated pecorino and a heavy grind of black pepper until it forms a thick paste.
Drain the pasta, reserving a mugful of the cooking water, and tip it into the pan with the bacon off the heat.
Stir the yolk mixture through immediately, loosening with splashes of pasta water until the sauce coats each strand.
Serve at once with more pecorino and pepper — it stiffens as it cools.

title: Spicy Arrabiata Penne
short_description: Angry red sauce: garlic, chilli and tomatoes, done in the time the pasta boils.
full_description: Arrabbiata means angry, and the heat is the point. The sauce is nothing more than garlic bloomed in good olive oil, chilli flakes, and a tin of tomatoes cooked down hard until it turns from watery to jammy. Everything happens in the window the penne needs, which makes it the most reliable weeknight pasta there is.

steps.text: Put the penne on to boil in heavily salted water.
Warm the olive oil in a wide pan and soften the sliced garlic gently — let it turn pale gold, not brown.
Add the chilli flakes and Italian seasoning and let them sizzle for a few seconds to release their oils.
Tip in the chopped tomatoes, season, and simmer hard until the sauce darkens and pulls away from the pan.
Toss the drained penne through the sauce, tear in the basil, and finish with grated Parmigiano-Reggiano.

title: Massaman Beef curry
short_description: Slow-braised Thai curry with peanuts, potato and warm whole spices.
full_description: Massaman sits apart from Thailand's other curries — it is mild, sweet and perfumed with cinnamon, closer in spirit to a Persian braise than a green curry. The beef needs two unhurried hours to give up and go tender, and the tamarind and palm sugar are what keep all that coconut cream from tasting flat. Roast the peanuts yourself; it is a small step that changes the whole dish.

ingredients.name: chilli
ingredients.note: red deseeded and finely sliced, to serve

steps.text: Roast the peanuts on a tray in a hot oven until golden, then cool and chop them roughly. Drop the oven to 180C.
Heat a few spoonfuls of the coconut cream in a casserole and fry the curry paste until it smells fragrant.
Stir in the beef and turn it until every piece is coated and sealed.
Pour in the remaining coconut cream with half a can of water, then add the potatoes, onion wedges, lime leaves and cinnamon stick.
Cover and braise in the oven until the beef shreds under a fork and the potatoes are soft.
Season with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce, balancing until it tastes sour, sweet and salty at once.
Scatter over the peanuts and sliced red chilli and serve with jasmine rice.

title: Tom yum soup with prawns
short_description: Hot-and-sour prawn broth sharpened with lemongrass, galangal and lime.
full_description: Tom yum is an exercise in balance rather than technique — the broth should hit sour, salty, hot and faintly sweet in that order, and you adjust it right up until it goes in the bowl. The aromatics are bruised rather than chopped so they perfume the stock without anyone having to eat a mouthful of lemongrass. A spoonful of chilli jam and a splash of coconut milk round off the edges.

gallery.alt_text: Tom yum soup with prawns, photograph 1
Tom yum soup with prawns, photograph 2

steps.text: Bruise the lemongrass stalks and slice the galangal, then simmer both in the stock with the lime leaves to build the base.
Add the onion and tomato wedges and cook until they just soften.
Stir in the chilli jam and coconut milk and bring back to a gentle simmer.
Drop in the prawns and oyster mushrooms and poach until the prawns turn opaque.
Take the pan off the heat before seasoning with fish sauce and lime juice — boiling dulls both.
Taste and adjust until it is aggressively sour and salty, then finish with coriander.

title: Beef Rendang
short_description: Dry Malaysian curry cooked down until the coconut caramelises onto the meat.
full_description: Rendang is not a saucy curry — it is cooked far past that point, until the coconut cream splits, the liquid disappears and what is left is a dark, almost dry paste clinging to the beef. That takes hours of patient stirring and cannot be rushed. The whole spices go in at the start and stay in, and the dish is genuinely better the next day.

steps.text: Blend the shallots into a paste and fry them in the oil with the cinnamon, cloves, star anise and cardamom until aromatic.
Add the beef and turn it in the spice paste until sealed on all sides.
Pour in the coconut cream and water, then add the tamarind paste, lime and sugar.
Simmer uncovered, stirring often, and let the liquid reduce right down.
Keep going past the point it looks done — the sauce should darken, split and cling to the meat.
Rest for at least ten minutes before serving; overnight is better still.

title: Beef pho
short_description: Vietnamese noodle soup with a charred-aromatic broth and raw sliced steak.
full_description: The broth is the dish. Charring the onion and ginger before they go in is what gives pho its depth and faint smokiness, and the whole spices should steep rather than boil. The steak is sliced thin and left raw in the bowl — the hot broth poured over the top cooks it in seconds, which is why it stays tender.

steps.text: Char the halved onion and ginger directly over a flame or under a hot grill until blackened in patches.
Toast the cinnamon, star anise, coriander seeds and cloves in a dry pan until they smell fragrant.
Add the charred aromatics and toasted spices to the beef stock and steep at the barest simmer.
Strain the broth, then season with fish sauce, soy sauce and palm sugar.
Soak the rice noodles until pliable and divide them between four deep bowls.
Lay the thinly sliced raw sirloin over the noodles and ladle the boiling broth straight on top.
Serve with spring onions, herbs, chilli and lime for everyone to add themselves.

title: Vegan banh mi
short_description: Crisp baguette, quick pickles and marinated tempeh — the meat-free banh mi.
full_description: A banh mi is a French colonial sandwich rebuilt around Vietnamese flavours, and it survives the switch to plants better than most. The quick pickle is doing the heavy lifting: sharp, sweet and still crunchy after twenty minutes in vinegar. Tempeh takes the place of pork because it browns properly and holds up to the bread instead of collapsing into it.

steps.text: Shred the raw vegetables finely and toss them with the vinegar and sugar. Leave them to pickle while you do everything else.
Slice the tempeh and fry it until deeply golden on both sides.
Split the baguette lengthways without cutting all the way through, and pull out a little of the soft crumb.
Spread the hummus thickly along the base.
Layer in the tempeh, drained pickles and a generous amount of coriander and mint.
Add hot sauce to taste and press the sandwich closed firmly before cutting.

title: Sweet and Sour Chicken
short_description: Crisp velveted chicken in a pineapple and ketchup glaze.
full_description: The technique worth stealing here is velveting — a brief coat of egg white and cornstarch that keeps the chicken juicy through high-heat cooking and gives it a lacquered surface for the sauce to grip. The sauce itself is unapologetically sweet, and the vinegar is what stops it being cloying, so do not cut it back.

steps.text: Cut the chicken thighs into bite-sized pieces and toss them with the egg white, salt and cornstarch. Rest for fifteen minutes.
Whisk the pineapple juice, vinegar, ketchup and brown sugar together and set the sauce aside.
Get a wok very hot, add the oil, and fry the chicken in batches until golden and cooked through.
Lift the chicken out, then stir-fry the peppers and ginger briefly so they keep some bite.
Return the chicken, pour in the sauce and add the pineapple chunks.
Bubble until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.

title: Kung Po Prawns
short_description: Fiery Sichuan-style prawns with peanuts and water chestnuts.
full_description: Everything in this dish is prepped before the wok gets hot, because once it does you have about four minutes total. The peanuts want to go in near the end so they stay crunchy, and the water chestnuts are there entirely for texture — they hold their snap no matter what you do to them.

steps.text: Toss the prawns with the soy sauce, tomato puree, corn flour and caster sugar and leave them to marinate.
Prepare everything else first — sliced chillies, chopped garlic, drained water chestnuts — and line it up by the hob.
Heat the sunflower oil in a wok until it shimmers, then fry the garlic and chillies for a few seconds only.
Add the prawns and stir-fry hard until they curl and turn pink.
Throw in the water chestnuts, peanuts and brown sugar and toss everything together for a final minute.

title: Ma Po Tofu
short_description: Silken tofu in a numbing Sichuan sauce with minced beef.
full_description: The name refers to the pockmarked face of the old woman said to have invented it, and the defining sensation is ma — the citrus-tingling numbness of Sichuan pepper, which is a different thing entirely from chilli heat. Doubanjiang, the fermented broad bean paste, is not optional; it is the entire backbone of the sauce. Handle the tofu gently and it will hold together.

steps.text: Cut the tofu into cubes and slide them into lightly salted warm water to firm up while you cook.
Toast the Sichuan pepper in a dry wok, then grind it coarsely and set it aside.
Brown the minced beef in the olive oil until it is properly crisp rather than just grey.
Add the doubanjiang, fermented black beans, garlic and ginger and fry until the oil turns red.
Pour in the water and soy sauce, then drain the tofu and slide it in, nudging rather than stirring.
Thicken with the cornstarch slurry, then finish with sesame oil, the ground Sichuan pepper and spring onions.

title: Katsu Chicken curry
short_description: Panko-crumbed chicken with a mellow, lightly sweet Japanese curry sauce.
full_description: Japanese curry owes more to British naval cooking than to India — it is thickened with a flour roux, barely spiced by South Asian standards, and rounded off with something sweet. Here the sauce is built from scratch rather than a block, and it is strained smooth, which is the step most people skip and the one that makes it taste bought.

steps.text: Soften the onions, garlic and carrot in the sunflower oil over a low heat until sweet.
Stir in the flour, curry powder and garam masala and cook out the raw taste.
Add the stock gradually, then the honey, soy sauce and bay leaf, and simmer until thickened.
Blend the sauce and pass it through a sieve — this is what makes it glossy rather than grainy.
Dredge the pounded chicken breasts in flour, then beaten egg, then breadcrumbs, pressing the crumbs on firmly.
Shallow-fry until deep golden and cooked through, then drain on kitchen paper.
Slice the katsu thickly and serve over rice with the sauce poured alongside.

title: Tonkatsu pork
short_description: Panko-crusted pork chops with a tangy brown tonkatsu sauce.
full_description: The crust is the whole point, and panko is what delivers it — the flakes are larger and drier than ordinary breadcrumbs, so they fry up jagged and stay crisp. The sauce is a four-ingredient cheat that lands remarkably close to the bottled version: ketchup for body, Worcestershire for sourness, oyster sauce for depth and sugar to pull it together.

steps.text: Stir the ketchup, Worcestershire sauce, oyster sauce and sugar together until the sugar dissolves. Set aside.
Bat the pork chops out to an even thickness and season them well on both sides.
Set up three bowls — flour, beaten egg, breadcrumbs — and coat each chop in that order.
Heat the oil to the point where a crumb sizzles immediately, then fry the chops until deep golden.
Rest on a rack rather than paper so the underside stays crisp.
Slice across into strips and serve with the sauce.

title: Japanese Katsudon
short_description: Pork cutlet simmered with onion and egg, served over rice.
full_description: Katsudon takes yesterday's tonkatsu and rescues it — the cutlet goes into a shallow pan of sweet-salty dashi with sliced onion, then beaten egg is poured over and left barely set. The rice underneath soaks up everything that runs off. It is a student dish, a hangover dish, and genuinely one of the best things you can do with leftovers.

steps.text: Cook the sushi rice and keep it warm and covered.
Slice the onion thinly and soften it in the oil in a small frying pan.
Add the stock, soy sauce, mirin and sugar and bring to a simmer.
Lay the chopped pork in the pan and let it warm through in the broth.
Pour the beaten eggs over the top and cover — take it off while they are still soft and barely set.
Slide the whole thing onto the rice and scatter with chives.

title: Sushi
short_description: Seasoned sushi rice rolled with cucumber and a spiced mayonnaise.
full_description: Everything hinges on the rice. It has to be rinsed until the water runs clear, cooked with a fraction less liquid than you would expect, then folded — never stirred — with seasoned rice wine while it cools. Get that right and the rolling is the easy part. Keep a bowl of water beside you; wet hands are the difference between rolling rice and wearing it.

steps.text: Rinse the sushi rice in several changes of cold water until it runs clear.
Cook the rice, then spread it out in a wide dish and fold the rice wine and sugar through with a cutting motion while it cools.
Stir the mayonnaise with the remaining rice wine and soy sauce to make the dressing.
Cut the cucumber into long batons, discarding the watery seed core.
Spread rice thinly over the nori, leaving a clear border along the far edge, and lay the cucumber across the near third.
Roll tightly away from you using the mat, sealing the border with a dab of water.
Slice with a wet blade, wiping between cuts, and serve with the spiced mayonnaise.

title: Lamb Tagine
short_description: Moroccan braise of lamb, apricots and squash with saffron and cinnamon.
full_description: A tagine should taste sweet and savoury at once, and the apricots are what bridge the two — they collapse into the sauce and thicken it as much as they flavour it. Saffron is the expensive ingredient and there is no substitute worth making; a quarter teaspoon is genuinely enough. Long, low heat does the rest.

steps.text: Brown the diced lamb hard in the olive oil, in batches, and lift it out.
Soften the onion and carrots in the same pan, scraping up everything stuck to the base.
Add the garlic, cumin, ginger, saffron and cinnamon and fry until the kitchen smells of them.
Return the lamb with the stock cube, honey and enough water to almost cover.
Cover and cook at a bare simmer until the lamb is yielding.
Add the apricots and butternut squash and cook until the squash is tender but still holds its shape.
Rest, then serve over steamed couscous with plenty of chopped parsley.

title: Chicken Couscous
short_description: One-pan harissa chicken with chickpeas, apricots and fluffy couscous.
full_description: Couscous is not cooked so much as hydrated — hot stock poured over, covered, and left alone for five minutes, then forked through. The harissa does all the seasoning work, so the quality of the paste matters more than anything else on the list. Dinner in under half an hour, in one pan.

steps.text: Soften the chopped onion in the olive oil until translucent.
Add the diced chicken breast and brown it lightly on all sides.
Stir in the harissa and ginger and coat everything well.
Add the chickpeas and chopped apricots with a splash of the stock and simmer until the chicken is cooked through.
Tip in the couscous, pour over the remaining hot stock, cover and take off the heat.
Fork the grains through to separate them and finish with torn coriander.

title: Lamb and Lemon Souvlaki
short_description: Charred lamb skewers marinated in garlic, lemon and dill.
full_description: Souvlaki is marinade and fire, nothing more. Salt the garlic and crush it to a paste rather than chopping it — it distributes properly that way and will not catch and burn on the grill. Leave the lamb in the lemon overnight if you can, but not much longer, or the acid starts to cure the outside of the meat.

steps.text: Crush the garlic to a paste with the sea salt using the flat of a knife.
Whisk it into the olive oil with the lemon zest and juice and the chopped dill.
Cube the lamb leg, turn it through the marinade, and refrigerate.
Thread onto skewers, leaving a little space between pieces so the heat gets around them.
Grill over a high heat, turning, until charred outside and pink within.
Rest briefly and serve stuffed into warm pita.

title: Chicken Quinoa Greek Salad
short_description: Warm quinoa with chilli-garlic chicken, feta, olives and mint.
full_description: A salad that eats like a main course. Quinoa is naturally bland, so it is cooked and then dressed while still warm, which is when it absorbs most — dress it cold and the seasoning just sits on the surface. The feta goes in at the very end so it crumbles rather than dissolves.

steps.text: Rinse the quinoa thoroughly — the coating on the outside is bitter — then cook it and let it steam dry.
Melt the butter with the olive oil and fry the chopped chilli and garlic briefly.
Add the sliced chicken breast and cook until golden and firm.
Fold the warm quinoa through the pan so it takes up the buttery juices.
Add the olives, red onion and lemon juice and toss.
Crumble the feta over at the last moment and finish with torn mint.

title: Turkish lahmacun
short_description: Paper-thin Turkish flatbread under a spiced minced lamb topping.
full_description: Lahmacun lives or dies on how thin you roll the base — it should be translucent enough to read through, and it bakes in four or five minutes in the hottest oven you own. The topping is spread raw and cooks in that same window, so everything in it must be chopped finely. Roll it up around salad and lemon and eat it with your hands.

steps.text: Mix the flour and yeast with warm water and salt, then knead until smooth and elastic.
Leave the dough covered somewhere warm until doubled.
Blitz the tomatoes, green chillies, spring onions, parsley and olive oil to a coarse paste.
Work the paste into the ground beef with the chilli flakes, cumin and allspice.
Heat the oven as high as it will go with a baking stone or heavy tray inside.
Roll each dough ball out paper-thin on a cornfloured surface and spread the topping right to the edge.
Bake until the edges blister and the meat is just cooked.
Serve with lemon wedges and sliced red onion to roll up inside.

title: Turkish lamb pilau
short_description: Spiced rice baked with lamb, apricots and toasted pine nuts.
full_description: A pilau is about the rice absorbing a flavoured stock without ever being stirred — stirring releases starch and you end up with risotto by accident. Toast the pine nuts separately and add them at the end, because they burn in the time the rice needs and there is no recovering from that.

steps.text: Toast the pine nuts in a dry pan until golden and tip them straight out — they carry on cooking in a hot pan.
Brown the diced lamb in the olive oil and set it aside.
Soften the chopped onion with the cinnamon sticks in the same pan.
Stir the rinsed basmati through the fat until every grain is coated and glossy.
Return the lamb, add the apricots and hot stock, cover tightly and cook without stirring.
Rest off the heat, still covered, then fork through with the pine nuts and mint.

title: Kumpir
short_description: Turkish street-food baked potato whipped with butter and cheese.
full_description: What separates kumpir from an ordinary jacket potato is what happens after it comes out of the oven: the flesh is mashed in the skin with butter and cheese until it is genuinely fluffy and emulsified, almost like a pommes puree in a jacket. Only then do the toppings go on. Skip that step and you have just made a baked potato.

steps.text: Prick the potatoes all over, rub them with salt, and bake until the skins are crisp and they give under pressure.
Split each one lengthways without cutting through the base.
Work the butter and grated cheese into the hot flesh with a fork, right there in the skin, until smooth and fluffy.
Pile on the chopped onion and red pepper.
Finish with a pinch of red chilli flakes.

title: Gambas al ajillo
short_description: Prawns sizzled in garlic chilli oil — five ingredients, six minutes.
full_description: This is a tapas bar standard that punishes hesitation. The oil needs to be properly hot and the garlic needs to go in just ahead of the prawns so it flavours the oil without burning. The prawns are done the moment they curl. Most of the pleasure is in the oil left behind, so serve it with bread that can mop.

steps.text: Slice the garlic thinly and halve the dried cayenne peppers.
Heat the olive oil in a small earthenware or heavy pan until it shimmers.
Add the garlic and chilli and let them sizzle for a few seconds only.
Slide in the prawns in a single layer and cook until they curl and turn opaque.
Scatter with parsley and take it to the table still spitting, with bread.

title: Ham croquetas
short_description: Molten jamón béchamel in a crisp fried shell.
full_description: The filling is a béchamel cooked far thicker than you would ever make for a sauce, then chilled until sliceable — that overnight rest in the fridge is not optional, and croquetas fail at the frying stage almost entirely because someone skipped it. Done properly the outside shatters and the inside is still liquid.

steps.text: Sweat the finely chopped leek in the olive oil until completely soft but uncoloured.
Add the chopped jamón and warm it through.
Stir in the flour and cook it out properly — a raw roux ruins the whole batch.
Add the milk and stock a little at a time, beating hard, until you have a very thick, smooth paste.
Season with grated nutmeg, spread into a shallow tray, cover and chill until firm.
Shape into barrels, then roll in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs.
Deep-fry in batches until deep gold, and drain on a rack.

title: Salt cod tortilla
short_description: Spanish potato omelette enriched with flakes of salt cod.
full_description: A tortilla is judged on its middle, which should be just short of set — baveuse, the French would say. The potatoes are poached gently in olive oil rather than fried crisp, which is what gives the finished tortilla its soft, almost creamy texture. Remember to soak the salt cod well in advance or the whole thing will be inedible.

steps.text: Soak the salt cod in several changes of cold water, then drain and flake it, discarding any skin and bone.
Slice the potatoes thinly and poach them gently in the olive oil with the onion until tender but not browned.
Add the chopped garlic for the last minute, then drain, reserving the oil.
Beat the eggs with the parsley, then fold through the warm potatoes and flaked cod. Rest the mixture.
Return a little oil to the pan and pour the mixture in, drawing the edges inward as it sets.
Invert onto a plate and slide it back in to finish the other side, keeping the centre soft.
Rest for ten minutes before cutting — it firms as it sits.

title: Padron peppers
short_description: Blistered Galician peppers with sea salt. Roughly one in ten bites back.
full_description: Two ingredients and a hot pan. Padrón peppers are picked young and are almost all mild, but a small fraction ripen hot enough to startle you, which is the game. They need a genuinely smoking pan so the skins blister before the flesh collapses, and they want more salt than feels reasonable.

steps.text: Wash the peppers and dry them completely — any water left on them will steam instead of blister.
Get a heavy frying pan properly smoking, then add the olive oil.
Throw the peppers in and leave them alone until the skins blacken in patches.
Toss and repeat until they are blistered all over and starting to slump.
Tip into a bowl and shower with flaky sea salt. Eat immediately with your fingers.

title: Chicken Enchilada Casserole
short_description: Layered tortillas, shredded chicken and Monterey Jack, baked until bubbling.
full_description: All the flavour of enchiladas without rolling a single one — the tortillas are layered flat like lasagne sheets, which takes about a fifth of the time and bakes more evenly. Four ingredients, one dish, and it reheats better than most things that come out of an oven.

steps.text: Poach the chicken breasts until cooked through, then shred them with two forks.
Heat the oven to 190C and spoon a thin layer of enchilada sauce over the base of a baking dish.
Lay down tortillas, then chicken, then sauce, then cheese — and repeat until everything is used.
Finish with a heavy layer of Monterey Jack on top.
Bake until the cheese is molten and blistered at the edges.
Rest for ten minutes before cutting or it will slide apart.

title: Cajun spiced fish tacos
short_description: Blackened white fish in soft tortillas with avocado and lime crema.
full_description: Cajun seasoning on a very hot pan gives the fish a dark, almost burnt-looking crust that is entirely the point — that is where the flavour is. Use a firm white fish that will not fall apart when you turn it, and assemble at the table so the tortillas do not go soggy waiting.

steps.text: Mix the cajun seasoning with the cayenne and rub it over the fish fillets on both sides.
Stir the garlic and a squeeze of lemon through the sour cream to make a quick crema.
Get a heavy pan very hot with the vegetable oil.
Sear the fish without moving it until a dark crust forms, then turn once.
Warm the tortillas briefly in a dry pan until flexible.
Flake the fish into the tortillas and top with lettuce, spring onion, avocado, salsa and crema.

title: Dal fry
short_description: Soft toor dal finished with a sizzling ghee tempering.
full_description: Dal fry is two operations. First the lentils are cooked to collapse with turmeric and salt — plain, almost dull. Then the tadka: whole spices bloomed in hot ghee and poured over at the last second, which is where every bit of the aroma comes from. Pour it over at the table if you want the theatre.

steps.text: Rinse the toor dal until the water runs clear, then simmer it with the water, salt and turmeric until completely soft.
Whisk the cooked dal briefly to break it down to a loose, creamy consistency.
Heat the ghee in a small pan and add the cumin and mustard seeds — wait for them to pop.
Add the bay leaves, green chilli and shredded ginger and fry until fragrant.
Stir in the chopped tomatoes and red pepper and cook until the fat separates out.
Pour the tempering into the dal, add the garam masala, and simmer briefly to bring it together.
Finish with chopped cilantro and a pinch of sugar to balance.

title: Baingan Bharta
short_description: Smoke-roasted aubergine mashed with tomato, garlic and green chilli.
full_description: The aubergine has to be charred over a naked flame until the skin is black and the inside has collapsed — an oven will cook it but will not give you the smoke, and the smoke is the dish. Once it is peeled the flesh is mashed rather than blended, because bharta should have texture.

steps.text: Rub the aubergine with a little oil and char it directly over a gas flame, turning, until the skin is blackened all over and it collapses.
Leave it to cool in a covered bowl — the trapped steam loosens the skin.
Peel away the burnt skin and mash the flesh coarsely with a fork.
Fry the garlic and green chilli in the remaining oil until golden.
Add the onion and cook until soft, then the tomatoes and red chilli powder.
Stir the mashed aubergine in and cook it down until the oil separates.
Season and finish with chopped coriander leaves.

title: Matar Paneer
short_description: Paneer and peas in a spiced tomato gravy.
full_description: Paneer does not melt, which is what makes it useful — it holds its shape through a simmer and takes on whatever it is cooked in. Fry the cubes first for colour and a firmer bite, though plenty of cooks add them straight in. The gravy wants cooking until the oil visibly separates; that is the signal it is done rather than merely hot.

steps.text: Cube the paneer and fry it in the sunflower oil until pale gold on each side, then lift it out.
Add the cumin to the same pan and let it crackle.
Grate in the ginger and green chilli, then add the chopped tomatoes with the turmeric and ground coriander.
Cook the gravy down hard until it darkens and the oil pools at the edges.
Add the peas and a splash of water and simmer until tender.
Return the paneer, add the garam masala, and warm through without boiling.
Scatter with coriander and serve with naan.

title: Full English Breakfast
short_description: The full plate: sausage, bacon, black pudding, eggs, beans and fried bread.
full_description: The difficulty here is not any individual component — it is getting nine of them onto a plate hot at the same time. The answer is sequencing: sausages first because they take longest, eggs last because they take seconds, and a low oven holding everything in between. Fry the bread in the bacon fat; it is the best thing on the plate.

steps.text: Start the sausages in a cold pan over a medium heat and turn them regularly — they need the longest.
Heat the oven low and use it to hold everything as it finishes.
Add the bacon to the pan and cook to your preference, then move it to the oven.
Halve the tomatoes and cook them cut-side down with the mushrooms and sliced black pudding.
Warm the baked beans through in a small pan.
Fry the bread in the rendered bacon fat until crisp and golden on both sides.
Fry the eggs last, basting with hot fat, and plate everything immediately.

title: Smoked Haddock Kedgeree
short_description: Anglo-Indian breakfast rice with smoked haddock and soft-boiled eggs.
full_description: Kedgeree came back from colonial India and settled into the British breakfast, which is why it is spiced so gently — turmeric for colour, cardamom and cinnamon for warmth, and not much heat at all. Poach the haddock in the stock you will cook the rice in; throwing that liquid away is throwing away the entire point.

steps.text: Poach the smoked haddock gently in the stock until it flakes, then lift it out and reserve the liquid.
Soft-boil the eggs, cool them under running water and peel.
Melt the butter and soften the chopped onion with the cardamom pods, cinnamon stick, bay and turmeric.
Stir the basmati through the spiced butter until the grains are coated.
Pour in the reserved poaching stock, cover, and cook without stirring until the liquid is absorbed.
Flake the haddock through the rice, keeping the pieces large.
Quarter the eggs over the top and finish with parsley and lemon.

title: Sticky Toffee Pudding
short_description: Date-free treacle sponge drowned in hot muscovado toffee sauce.
full_description: The sponge is deliberately plain and slightly bitter from the black treacle and bicarbonate, because it exists to carry the sauce rather than compete with it. Make half again as much sauce as you think you need — it should pool. Both parts reheat well, which makes this a genuinely good dinner-party pudding.

steps.text: Heat the oven to 180C and butter a deep baking dish.
Cream the butter and muscovado sugar until light, then beat in the eggs one at a time.
Fold in the flour, baking powder and bicarbonate, then the black treacle and milk — the batter will be very loose.
Pour into the dish and bake until risen and springy in the centre.
For the sauce, melt the butter, muscovado sugar and treacle together, then stir in the cream and vanilla.
Simmer until it thickens and darkens slightly.
Prick the hot sponge all over and pour a third of the sauce in, serving the rest at the table with cream.

title: Eton Mess
short_description: Crushed meringue, strawberries and whipped cream. Assembled, not cooked.
full_description: There is no technique to defend here — the only real decision is when to assemble, and the answer is at the last possible moment, because the meringue starts dissolving on contact. Macerating half the strawberries with a little ginger cordial and crushing them into a rough sauce gives it the ripple that plain chopped fruit will not.

steps.text: Hull the strawberries. Set half aside and roughly crush the rest with the ginger cordial.
Leave the crushed fruit to macerate and release its juice.
Whip the double cream to soft peaks — stop well before it stiffens.
Break the meringue nests into uneven pieces, keeping some large.
Fold the cream, meringue, chopped strawberries and crushed fruit together in three or four strokes only.
Spoon into glasses and top with a sprig of mint. Serve straight away.

title: Bakewell tart
short_description: Shortcrust shell, raspberry jam and almond frangipane under flaked almonds.
full_description: Blind-baking the shell is what stops the base going grey and soggy under the jam, and it is the step worth being fussy about. The frangipane rises as it bakes and then settles, so spread it level rather than domed. Almond extract is potent — half a teaspoon really is enough.

steps.text: Rub the chilled butter into the flour until it resembles breadcrumbs, then bring it together with the cold water.
Wrap and chill the pastry before rolling — warm pastry shrinks in the tin.
Line the tart tin, prick the base, and blind-bake with beans until pale gold and dry.
Beat the butter and caster sugar together, then work in the ground almonds, beaten egg and almond extract.
Spread the raspberry jam over the cooled base and level the frangipane over it.
Scatter with flaked almonds and bake until risen, firm and golden.
Cool in the tin — it is too fragile to move while hot.

title: Vegan Chocolate Cake
short_description: One-bowl chocolate cake with flax eggs and almond milk.
full_description: No dairy, no eggs, and — if you are careful about the flour — no reason anyone needs to be told. The boiling water at the end looks like a mistake; it is not. It blooms the cacao and thins the batter right down, which is exactly what gives this cake its tight, damp crumb.

steps.text: Make the flax eggs by stirring ground flaxseed into water and leaving them to thicken to a gel.
Heat the oven to 180C and line a round cake tin.
Whisk the self-raising flour, coco sugar, raw cacao and baking powder together in one bowl.
Stir in the flax eggs, almond milk and vanilla until just combined — do not beat it.
Pour in the boiling water last and mix to a very thin batter.
Bake until a skewer comes out with a few damp crumbs rather than clean.
Cool in the tin for ten minutes before turning out.
